Ancient Armenia — a multilingual (hy/ru/en/pt) offline guide to the history of Armenia: Urartu-Armenia (782 BC) and Ancient Armenia from Alexander to Cilicia. Works without internet.

How to get there on foot
How to get there by car
From Yerevan center: take bus 16 or trolleybus 2 to Arin-Berd stop (south-east, ~20 min). Walk uphill 300 m following signs to the museum entrance.
From Republic Square: head south on Vardanants St, turn right onto Artashat Hwy, continue 4 km, turn left at Arin-Berd sign, follow the road uphill to the museum parking.
From Yerevan center: take bus 5 or 32 to Karmir Blur stop (west, ~15 min). The excavated citadel is visible from the main road, 200 m walk north.
From Republic Square: head west on Tigran Mets Ave, cross the Hrazdan bridge, continue on Erebuni Hwy 2.5 km, turn right at Karmir Blur sign.

From Urartu to the excavations: 860 BC → 20th century
The kingdom of Urartu takes shape
Tribal leagues of the Armenian Highland unite against Assyria; around 860 BC the core of the future kingdom emerges.
The capital is established at Tushpa (Van) by the lake; the earliest Urartian inscription names Sarduri, son of Lutipri.
The king captures Musasir, the sacred city of the god Haldi, and carves long inscriptions on the Van rock.
The Menua canal carries water to this day; dozens of fortresses and 50 km of irrigation canals transform the highland.
Argishti I founds the Erebuni fortress on the Arin-Berd hill — the conventional birth date of Yerevan, attested by a cuneiform inscription.
Urartu reaches its military and constructive zenith; its influence stretches from Anatolia to the southern Caucasus.
Tiglath-Pileser III defeats Sarduri II; the long decline of the kingdom begins.
Sargon II plunders the temple of Haldi at Musasir — an event described in detail in the Assyrian annals.
The last great fortress of the kingdom rises on Karmir Blur hill, dedicated to the god Teisheba.
Medes and Scythians destroy the kingdom; Teishebaini perishes in a great fire around 590 BC.
The highland joins the Achaemenid satrapy (Orontid dynasty); the following centuries bring Hellenism.
Boris Piotrovsky reveals Teishebaini: citadel, granaries and thousands of cuneiform tablets.
Konstantine Hovhannisyan unearths Erebuni; the palace murals establish Urartology as a discipline.
The fortresses of Erebuni and Teishebaini, the kings of Urartu, the gods Haldi and Teisheba. 860–590 BC.
Garni and Etchmiadzin, Tigranes the Great and Mashtots, Ani and Cilicia. Antiquity and the Middle Ages.
331 BC → AD 1375: from Alexander to the fall of Cilicia
Alexander\'s conquest shatters the Achaemenid Empire; the Orontid (Yervanduni) dynasty rules Armenia — first as satraps, then as kings.
Artashes I proclaims independence and founds the Artaxiad dynasty; tradition says the new capital Artashat was laid out with the help of Hannibal.
Tigranes II takes the title \'king of kings\'; the Armenian empire stretches from the Caspian to the Mediterranean with Tigranocerta as its new capital.
Lucullus besieges Tigranocerta; the pendulum swings, and Armenia becomes a buffer state between Rome and Parthia.
Pompey restores Tigranes as \'friend and ally of the Roman people\'; Armenia keeps its kings under Roman patronage.
Trdat I founds the Armenian Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty, linked by blood to Parthia.
Trdat III proclaims Christianity the state faith — the first Christian state in the world; Gregory the Illuminator, freed from Khor Virap, becomes the first Catholicos at Etchmiadzin.
The 36-letter Armenian alphabet gives the nation its script; the age of translation begins and with it the schools, the first books and an identity that outlives empires.
The Sasanians abolish the Armenian kingdom; marzpans rule in the shah\'s name, but the church keeps the nation together.
Vardan Mamikonian falls fighting the Sasanian army; the faith survives, and in 484 the Treaty of Nvarsak grants Armenia religious freedom.
Ashot I Bagratuni is crowned king of all Armenia — recognized by both Byzantium and the Caliphate.
Ashot III moves the throne to Ani; the city booms into a hub of trade, architecture and scholarship on the Akhurian gorge.
Byzantium annexes Ani; the Bagratid kingdom ends and Armenian statehood shifts west, to Cilicia.
The Mamluks take the last Armenian strongholds; Levon V is the final crowned king — the Middle Ages close.
After the war of Vahan Mamikonian the Sasanians grant Armenia freedom of faith — the harvest of Avarayr.
The Caliphate takes Armenia; princes like Theodore Rshtuni preserve wide autonomy under the ostikans.
Mongol armies take Ani and Kars; the Zakarian age ends and heavy tribute follows.
A long walk: ~6 hours along the Geghard highway by the Azat gorge. Bus 266 from Yerevan or a taxi is the realistic option.
From Republic Square take Khorenatsi St to the M2 highway, 28 km east, then 4 km left to Garni village.
From Garni a footpath runs 7 km up the Azat gorge to the monastery (~1.5 h).
Past Garni follow the road up the Azat gorge for another ~9 km to the monastery gate.
A 20 km walk west along the Yerevan highway — for hikers only.
From Republic Square go west via Tigran Mets Ave and the Argavand highway, 20 km to Vagharshapat; Zvartnots is 3 km before it.
From the Sevan town shore a paved path climbs the peninsula causeway (~30 min).
From Yerevan take the M4 highway north-east along the Hrazdan river, 65 km to Sevan town, then the peninsula road.
A full-day hike through the Vorotan gorge from Tatev village down the switchbacks (~2 h one way).
From Yerevan the Yerevan-Goris highway south, then via Sisian and the Vorotan gorge road; or ride the Wings of Tatev cableway from Halidzor.
A flat 30 km walk south through Ararat villages — bikes or buses 456/467 from Yerevan are easier.
From Yerevan south on the M2 toward Ararat city, 30 km, then right to Pokr Vedi village; the monastery is visible from far away.
